documentNotes.title: Native editorial preface
documentNotes.statement:
Preface
Preface
Preface
Preface 
This publication contains the competition problems (Volume 2) from the 21st – 40th 
International Chemistry Olympiads (IChO) organized in the years 1989 – 2008  and is a 
continuation of the publication that appeared last year as Volume 1 and contained 
competition problems from the first twenty IChOs.  The whole review of the competition 
tasks set in the IChO in its fourty-year history is a contribution of the IChO International 
Information Centre in Bratislava (Slovakia) to the development of this world known 
international competition. This Volume 2 contains 154 theoretical and 46 practical 
competition problems from the mentioned years. The review as a whole presents 
altogether 279 theoretical and 96 practical problems.  
In the elaboration of this collection the editor had to face certain difficulties because 
the aim was not only to make use of past recordings but also to give them such a form 
that they may be used in practice and further chemical education. Consequently, it was 
necessary to make some corrections in order to unify the form of the problems. However, 
they did not concern the contents and language of the problems.  
Unfortunately, the authors of the particular competition problems are not known and 
due to the procedure of the creation of the IChO competition problems, it is impossible to 
assign any author's name to a particular problem. As the editor I would appreciate many  
times some discussion with the authors about any critical places that occurred in the text. 
On the other hand, any additional amendments to the text would be not correct from the  
historical point of view. Therefore, responsibility for the scientific content and language of 
the problems lies exclusively with the organizers of the particular International Chemistry 
Olympiads.    
 
Some parts of texts, especially those gained as scanned materials, could not be 
used directly and thus, several texts, schemes and pictures had to be re-written or created 
again. Some solutions were often available in a brief form and necessary extent only, just 
for the needs of members of the International Jury.  
 
Recalculations of the solutions were made in some special cases only when the 
numeric results in the original solutions showed to be obviously not correct. Although the 
numbers of significant figures in the results of several solutions do not obey the criteria 
generally accepted, they were left without change.      


 
In this publication SI quantities and units are used and a more modern method of 
chemical calculations is introduced. Only some exceptions have been made when, in an 
effort to preserve the original text, the quantities and units have been used that are not SI.  
There were some problems with the presentation of the solutions of practical tasks, 
because most of the relatively simple calculations were based on the experimental results 
of contestants. Moreover, the practical problems are accompanied with answer sheets in 
the last years and several additional questions and tasks have appeared in them that were 
not a part of the text of the original experimental problems. Naturally, answer sheets could 
not be included in this publication and can only be preserved as archive materials. 
  
When reading the texts of the IChO problems one must admire and appreciate the 
work of those many known and unknown people – teachers, authors, pupils, and 
organizers – who contributed so much to development and success of this important 
international competition. 
 
I am sure about the usefulness of the this review of the IChO problems. It may serve 
not only as archive material but, in particular, this review should serve to both competitors 
and their teachers as a source of further inspiration in their preparation for this challenging 
competition. 
 
 
 
 
Bratislava, July 2009  
 
 
 
 
 
 
  
 
                                    Anton Sirota, editor

problems.title: 1. Tellurium chloroaluminate catalysts
problems.statement:
The stereoregular polymerization of unsaturated hydrocarbons is usually considered as one of the most important for the industrial organic chemistry. The salts of big nonlinear cations carrying a sufficiently high charge to attack the electron density distributed along the $\pi$-bonds of the olefin molecules are usually used as catalysts in these processes. Chloroaluminate anions (like $\mathrm{AlCl_4^-}$) possessing a highly delocalized negative charge are usually used as anions.

The necessity to develop new catalysts of this kind urged chemists to study the interaction in the system A–B, where A=$\mathrm{Te(cryst.)}$ and B=$\mathrm{(TeCl_4+4AlCl_3)}$. The second component B was considered as an analog of Te(IV) chloroaluminate $\mathrm{Te[AlCl_4]_4}$, which cannot be isolated as an individual compound. Interaction of components A and B can form three new compounds I, II and III in systems initially containing77.8,87.5 and91.7mol.% of component A, respectively. While II and III formed no side products, formation of I was accompanied by evolution of1mol volatile $\mathrm{TeCl_4}$ per2mol I.

I and II attracted particular interest. Both are pinkish-purple and dissociate into three ions as conductivity studies in melted $\mathrm{NaAlCl_4}$ showed. Cryoscopic measurements in the $\mathrm{NaAlCl_4}$ melt gave molecular weights $1126\pm43\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ for I and $867\pm48\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}$ for II. In both IR spectra only one band can be attributed to a vibration mode of a bond formed by Te. This band lies at $133\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, so low in energy that the bond undoubtedly is a kind of Te–Te interaction. The $^{27}\mathrm{Al}$ NMR data show only one type of tetrahedrally coordinated aluminum in each compound. The observed aluminium chemical shifts differ between I and II, manifesting that their Al atoms are different.

sections.title: Tasks

parts.statement: Determine the minimal Te:Al:Cl atomic ratio for complexes I, II and III.
Write the molecular formulae of compounds I and II.
Write the formulae of the anions and cations in compounds I and II.
Draw stereochemical formulae of cations and anions in the structures of I and II, assuming the cations in I and II are examples of inorganic aromatic systems.
Which compound has higher thermal stability, I or II, taking into account that $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ is extremely volatile?
If one of I or II can be transformed into the other by heating, write the corresponding reaction equation.

sections.statement:
| Compound | Te:Al:Cl |
| --- | --- |
| I | 2:2:7 |
| II | 2:1:4 |
| III | 3:1:4 |

The ratios can be determined from the content of Te(cryst.). The source prints that77.8% corresponds to $\mathrm{Te(cryst.)+2TeCl_4+8AlCl_3}$ and that the minimum atomic ratio before subtracting excess $\mathrm{TeCl_4}$ is9:8:32. Al and Cl contents are even and divisible by4, while Te exceeds the analogous even number by1. Subtracting1mol $\mathrm{TeCl_4}$ and dividing by2 gives $\mathrm{4Te+4Al+14Cl}$ and ratio2:2:7, verified against the given molecular weight.

87.5% corresponds to $\mathrm{7Te(cryst.)+TeCl_4+4AlCl_3=8Te+4Al+16Cl}$, giving2:1:4.91.7% corresponds to $\mathrm{11Te(cryst.)+TeCl_4+4AlCl_3=12Te+4Al+16Cl}$, giving3:1:4.

I:$\mathrm{Te_4Al_4Cl_{14}}$. II:$\mathrm{Te_4Al_2Cl_8}$.

The molecular formulae follow from molar weights. Both correspond to twice the simplest formula. For I, $2(\mathrm{Te_2Al_2Cl_7})$ gives calculated $M_r=1114.7$, compared with $1126\pm43$. For II, $2(\mathrm{Te_2AlCl_4})$ gives calculated $M_r=848$, compared with $867\pm48$.

I: cation $\mathrm{[Te_4]^{2+}}$, anion $\mathrm{[Al_2Cl_7]^-}$. II: cation $\mathrm{[Te_4]^{2+}}$, anion $\mathrm{[AlCl_4]^-}$.

Both I and II are tri-ionic electrolytes; all tellurium atoms should be equivalent according to IR and bonded only to each other. Al atoms are tetrahedrally coordinated and equivalent in both. At least one case can contain $\mathrm{AlCl_4^-}$, probable for II, formulated as $\mathrm{[Te_4]^{2+}[AlCl_4]_2^-}$ in the source. Similar colour suggests identical cations; I then contains $\mathrm{[Te_4]^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{[Al_2Cl_7]^-}$, agreeing with NMR that assigns I a tetrahedral geometry different from II.

$\mathrm{[Te_4]^{2+}}$ is a plane square due to proclaimed aromaticity. An aromatic cation is planar with equal bond lengths along the sides of its aromatic ring, favouring this configuration.

$\mathrm{AlCl_4^-}$ is a single tetrahedron. $\mathrm{Al_2Cl_7^-}$ consists of two tetrahedra sharing a common vertex (a chlorine atom).

II should have higher thermal stability. Both are ionic compounds with high melting points, but I can transform into II by eliminating $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$, a volatile solid relatively easily removed on heating.
$$\mathrm{Te_4[Al_2Cl_7]_2=Te_4[AlCl_4]_2+2AlCl_3}.$$

problems.title: 2. Detection limit and multiplicative bismuth analysis
problems.statement: The detection limit is one of the basic parameters in quantitative analysis of trace amounts of elements: the least mass of an element determined by a method with given accuracy. Consider the determination of microscopic amounts of bismuth. In1927 German chemist Berg suggested precipitating bismuth as practically insoluble8-hydroxyquinolinium tetraiodobismuthate, $\mathrm{[C_9H_6(OH)NH][BiI_4]}$, $M_r=862.7$.

sections.title: Tasks

parts.statement: a) Draw structural formulae of the cation and anion of this salt. b) What is the oxidation state of Bi?

Evaluate the smallest reliably determined mass of bismuth in mg by Berg's method, if the smallest reliably measured precipitate mass is50.0mg.

For trace bismuth, R.Belcher and co-workers from Birmingham developed a multiplicative method: a chain of reactions followed by titration of the final product. A detailed description follows.

Step1: To approximately $2\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ cold acidified solution containing trace $\mathrm{Bi^{3+}}$, add50mg potassium hexathiocyanatochromate(III), $\mathrm{K_3[Cr(SCN)_6]}$, in the cold. Bismuth precipitation is practically quantitative.

Write a balanced net ionic equation of this reaction.

Step2: Filter off the precipitate, wash with cold water, and treat with $5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$10% sodium hydrogen carbonate. The precipitate transforms to oxobismuth(III) carbonate, $\mathrm{(BiO)_2CO_3}$, releasing hexathiocyanatochromate(III) ions into solution.

Write a balanced net ionic equation of this reaction.

Step3: Transfer the slightly acidified filtrate to a separatory funnel, add $0.5\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ saturated iodine solution in chloroform, and shake vigorously. Iodine oxidizes the complex ligand to ICN and sulphate.

Write a balanced net ionic equation of this reaction.

Step4: After5min add $4\ \mathrm{cm^3}$2M $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$. Acidification causes coproportionation with evolution of molecular iodine.

Write a balanced net ionic equation of the reaction on acidification.

Step5: Quantitatively extract iodine with4portions of chloroform. Transfer the aqueous layer to a flask, add $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ bromine water and mix5min.

Write balanced net ionic equations upon addition of bromine water. Excess bromine can react with hydrogen cyanide to give BrCN, and iodide is oxidized to $\mathrm{IO_3^-}$.

Step6: Eliminate excess molecular bromine by adding $3\ \mathrm{cm^3}$90% methanoic(formic) acid.

Write a balanced net ionic equation of this reaction.

Step7: Add excess(1.5g) potassium iodide to the slightly acidic solution.

Write balanced net ionic equations upon addition of KI, considering that iodide reacts with BrCN similarly to ICN, forming molecular iodine.

Step8: Titrate the resulting solution with standard0.00200M $\mathrm{Na_2S_2O_3}$ and use the results to calculate sample bismuth content.

a) How many moles of thiosulphate are equivalent to1mol initial bismuth? b) What is the least determined bismuth mass, assuming reliable determination requires at least $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ standard0.00200M $\mathrm{Na_2S_2O_3}$?
How many times more sensitive is this multiplicative method than Berg's gravimetric method?

problems.title: 3. Radium decay and Avogadro's number
problems.statement:
In1908 Rutherford and H.Geiger measured the emission rate $x$ of $\alpha$-particles by radium, represented in nature by the single nuclide $^{226}_{88}\mathrm{Ra}$. They found1.00g emits $x=3.42\times10^{10}$particles per second.

In1911 Rutherford and American physical chemist B.Boltwood measured helium formation from radium. This permitted the most accurate Avogadro number then available, given the well-established ideal-gas molar volume. A radium-salt sample purified from decay products, containing $m=192$mg Ra, was put into a device and evolved helium measured. After $t=83.0$days, $V_{\mathrm{He}}=6.58\ \mathrm{mm^3}$ helium was collected, corrected to $0\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and1atm.

The kinetic scheme below gives half-lives above arrows and decay types below. RaA–RaE are intermediate radon-decay products.

![](p3-fig1)

sections.title: Tasks

parts.statement:
Write the first six radioactive decays using modern notation showing atomic and mass numbers of all nuclei.

As a rough first approximation, half-lives of all radium decay products except RaD and Po may be neglected against measurement time $t$. Use this approximation below.
a) How many helium atoms formed from each decayed radium atom after83days? b) How many formed in total?

Calculate an approximate Avogadro number from these data.

For a more accurate computation, radon's half-life $T_{1/2}(\mathrm{Rn})=3.83$days cannot be neglected, because it is comparable with $t$ and not all radon atoms have decayed by the experiment's end.

Choose which plot displays the time dependence of radon atom number $N_{\mathrm{Rn}}$ during the experiment.

![](p3-fig2)

Choose which plot shows the time dependence of helium volume during the experiment.

![](p3-fig3)
Choose the relation between decay rate $k$ of a nuclide and its half-life $T_{1/2}$.

a) Using the short scheme $\mathrm{Ra}\xrightarrow{k_1}\mathrm{Rn}\xrightarrow{k_2}\mathrm{RaA}$, where $k_1,k_2$ are rate constants, and the plot selected in question4, write a relation between radon number at the end $N'_{\mathrm{Rn}}$ and radium number $N_{\mathrm{Ra}}$.

b) Calculate $N'_{\mathrm{Rn}}$ using $x=3.42\times10^{10}$ $\alpha$-particles per gram radium per second.
How many helium atoms could form from the remaining $N'_{\mathrm{Rn}}$ radon atoms if all decayed to RaD?
Using the answers above, calculate better approximations to a) helium atom number and b) Avogadro number.

C. Radon atom number reaches a quasi-stationary state, sometimes called radioactive equilibrium.
F. Initially helium forms only from radium's $\alpha$-particles; by the end, radium and decay products emit them, the amount being four times that of radium.

Printed choices:$4N'_{\mathrm{Rn}}$, $2N'_{\mathrm{Rn}}$, $5N'_{\mathrm{Rn}}$, $N'_{\mathrm{Rn}}$, $3N'_{\mathrm{Rn}}$. The last is underlined.

$$N_{\mathrm{He}}=4xmt-3N'_{\mathrm{Rn}}=1.9\times10^{17}-3\times3.14\times10^{15}=1.79\times10^{17}.$$

problems.title: 4. Chromate equilibria and separation by precipitation
problems.statement:
Precipitation is widely used in classical quantitative and qualitative analysis for ion separation. Separation depends on equilibrium concentrations of all species in the solution. Potassium dichromate is widely used as a precipitating reagent. Aqueous Cr(VI) establishes:

$$\mathrm{HCrO_4^-\rightleftharpoons H^++CrO_4^{2-}},\qquad\log K_1=-6.50,$$

$$\mathrm{2HCrO_4^-\rightleftharpoons Cr_2O_7^{2-}+H_2O},\qquad\log K_2=1.36.$$

sections.title: Tasks

parts.statement:
Calculate equilibrium constants:

a) $\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}+H_2O\rightleftharpoons HCrO_4^-+OH^-}$.

b) $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}+2OH^-\rightleftharpoons2CrO_4^{2-}+H_2O}$.

Water's ionic product:$K_W=1.0\times10^{-14}$.

In what direction does equilibrium1(b) shift upon adding a) KOH,b) HCl,c) $\mathrm{BaCl_2}$,d) $\mathrm{H_2O}$ to aqueous potassium dichromate? $K_{sp}(\mathrm{BaCrO_4})=1.2\times10^{-10}$; $\mathrm{BaCr_2O_7}$ is well soluble in water.
Calculate pH of a)0.010M $\mathrm{K_2CrO_4}$,b)0.010M $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$,c)0.010M $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$+0.100M $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$. Acetic acid dissociation constant:$K_a=1.8\times10^{-5}$.

Calculate equilibrium concentrations of a) $\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}$ and b) $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$ in0.010M $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$+0.100M $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$.

a) Shall $\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ precipitate? b) Shall $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ precipitate? c) Shall quantitative separation be achieved? Quantitative precipitation requires residual concentration of the precipitated ion no higher than $1\times10^{-6}$M.

a) and b) are self-evident. c) Barium binds chromate into a poorly soluble compound:$\mathrm{Ba^{2+}+CrO_4^{2-}\to BaCrO_4}$.

d) Though water appears among products, that is too formal. In dilute aqueous solution water concentration can be regarded as constant and adding water does not affect it. Adding water does dilute the dichromate solution, shifting dissociation right. Also aqueous $\mathrm{K_2Cr_2O_7}$ has pH below7 from the processes described (compare solution3(b)). Dilution moves pH toward7, increasing pH here and shifting equilibrium right.

a) pH9.25,b)4.20,c)2.87.

a) $\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}+H_2O=HCrO_4^-+OH^-}$,$K=3.16\times10^{-8}$.

$$c_{\mathrm{Cr}}=[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]+[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]+2[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}]\approx[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}],\qquad[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]\approx[\mathrm{OH^-}].$$

$$\frac{[\mathrm{OH^-}]^2}{c_{\mathrm{Cr}}}=K,\qquad[\mathrm{OH^-}]=\sqrt{Kc_{\mathrm{Cr}}}=\sqrt{3.16\times10^{-8}\times0.01}=1.78\times10^{-5}.$$

$[\mathrm{H^+}]=5.65\times10^{-10}$,pH9.25.

b) $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}+H_2O=2HCrO_4^-}$,$K=1/K_2=4.37\times10^{-2}$. $\mathrm{HCrO_4^-=H^++CrO_4^{2-}}$,$K=K_1=3.16\times10^{-7}$.

The source sets $[\mathrm{H^+}]\approx[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]$ and prints a radicand containing $[\mathrm{HCrO_4^{2-}}]$:

$$[\mathrm{H^+}]=\sqrt{K_1[\mathrm{HCrO_4^{2-}}]}.$$

Find $[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]$ using

$$c_{\mathrm{Cr}}=2.0\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm M\ (**)=[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]+[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]+2[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}]\approx[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]+2[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}].$$

Set $[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]=x$,$K_2=[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}]/[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]^2=(c_{\mathrm{Cr}}-x)/(2x^2)$; thus $2K_2x^2+x-c_{\mathrm{Cr}}=0$.

Hence $[\mathrm{H^+}]=(3.16\times10^{-7}\times1.27\times10^{-2})^{1/2}=6.33\times10^{-5}$,pH4.20.

c) In0.10M acetic acid,$[\mathrm{H^+}]=(K_ac)^{1/2}$ (*) $=(1.8\times10^{-5}\times0.10)^{1/2}=1.34\times10^{-3}$;pH2.87.

a) $3.0\times10^{-6}$,b) $3.7\times10^{-3}$.

Different methods can be used.

**Method1.** a) $[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]=1.3\times10^{-2}$ (*).

$$[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]=\frac{K_1[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]}{[\mathrm{H^+}]}=\frac{3.16\times10^{-7}\times1.3\times10^{-2}}{1.34\times10^{-3}}=3.0\times10^{-6}.$$

b) $c_{\mathrm{Cr}}=[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]+[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]+2[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}]$.

$$[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}]=\tfrac12(c_{\mathrm{Cr}}-[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]-[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}])=\tfrac12(2.0\times10^{-2}-3.0\times10^{-6}-1.3\times10^{-2})=3.7\times10^{-3}.$$

Alternatively $[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}]=K_2[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]^2=22.9(1.3\times10^{-2})^2=3.9\times10^{-3}$.

**Method2.** a) Set $[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]=x$,$[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]=x[\mathrm{H^+}]/K_1$.

The printed line is $[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}]=K_2[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]=x^2K_2[\mathrm{H^+}]^2/K_1^2$.

$$c_{\mathrm{Cr}}=[\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}]+[\mathrm{HCrO_4^-}]+2[\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}]=\frac{2K_2[\mathrm{H^+}]^2}{K_1^2}x^2+\left(1+\frac{[\mathrm{H^+}]}{K_1}\right)x.$$

$K_1=3.16\times10^{-7}$,$K_2=22.9$,$[\mathrm{H^+}]=1.34\times10^{-3}$.

$$8.24\times10^8x^2+4.24\times10^3x-2.0\times10^{-2}=0,\qquad x=3.0\times10^{-6}.$$

problems.title: 5. Iron potentiometry and spectrophotometry
problems.statement:
Potentiometric and spectrophotometric methods widely determine equilibrium concentrations and constants in solution. Combining them frequently allows simultaneous determination of several species.

Solution I contains aqueous $\mathrm{FeCl_2}$ and $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$; II contains $\mathrm{K_4Fe(CN)_6}$ and $\mathrm{K_3Fe(CN)_6}$. Iron-containing concentrations satisfy $[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]_{\mathrm I}=[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{4-}}]_{\mathrm{II}}$ and $[\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}]_{\mathrm I}=[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}}]_{\mathrm{II}}$.

Platinum-electrode potential is0.652V in I and0.242V in II. Transmittance of II relative to I at420nm is10.7%; optical path $l=5.02$mm. $\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{4-}}$, $\mathrm{Fe(H_2O)_6^{3+}}$ and $\mathrm{Fe(H_2O)_6^{2+}}$ do not absorb at420nm. Molar absorption $\varepsilon([\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}}])=1100\ \mathrm{M^{-1}cm^{-1}}$. Standard potential for $\mathrm{Fe(H_2O)_6^{3+}/Fe(H_2O)_6^{2+}}$ is0.771V. The Nernst pre-logarithm factor is0.0590.

sections.title: Tasks

parts.statement: Write Nernst equations for a) solution I and b) solution II.
What are the units of the Nernst pre-logarithm factor0.0590?
Calculate $\beta[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}}]/\beta[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{4-}}]$.
What is the absolute variation range of a) transmittance $T$ and b) absorbance $A$?
Sketch concentration-dependence graphs obeying Lambert–Beer law for a) $A$,b) $T$,c) molar absorption $\varepsilon$.
Calculate concentrations of a) $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ in I,b) $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ in II.
Mixing I and II gives intense blue colour. Which species has this colour? Write the reaction equation.

sections.statement:
a) $E_{\mathrm I}=E^{\circ}(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}})+0.0590\log([\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}]/[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}])$.

b) The printed left side is also $E_{\mathrm I}$:

$$E_{\mathrm I}=E^{\circ}(\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}/Fe(CN)_6^{4-}})+0.0590\log\frac{[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}}]}{[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{4-}}]}.$$
V.

$\beta\{\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}}\}/\beta\{\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{4-}}\}=8.90\times10^6$.

Calculations:

$$E_{\mathrm{II}}=E^{\circ}(\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}/Fe(CN)_6^{4-}})+0.0590\log[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}/Fe(CN)_6^{4-}}]$$

$$=E^{\circ}(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}})+0.0590\log(\beta_1/\beta_2)+0.0590\log([\mathrm{CN^-}]^6/[\mathrm{CN^-}]^6)+0.0590\log[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}/Fe(CN)_6^{4-}}]=0.242.$$

$\beta_1,\beta_2$ are stability constants for $\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{4-}}$, $\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}}$, respectively. Since $[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}}]/[\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{4-}}]=[\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}]/[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]$,

$$\Delta E=E_{\mathrm{II}}-E_{\mathrm I}=0.0590\log(\beta_1/\beta_2),\qquad\beta_2/\beta_1=8.90\times10^6.$$
a)0to100. b)0to $\infty$.
![](p5-sol-fig1)

a) Using Bouger–Lambert–Beer law:

$$A=\varepsilon lc=0.971,\qquad c([\mathrm{Fe(CN)_6^{3-}}])=\frac{0.971}{1100\times0.502}=1.76\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm M=c([\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}]).$$

b) Using Nernst's equation:

$$E=E^{\circ}(\mathrm{Fe^{3+}/Fe^{2+}})+0.0590\log\frac{[\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}]_{\mathrm I}}{[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]_{\mathrm I}}=0.771+0.0590\log\frac{[\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}]_{\mathrm I}}{[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]_{\mathrm I}}=0.652\ \mathrm V.$$

Hence $[\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}]_{\mathrm I}/[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]_{\mathrm I}=9.62\times10^{-3}$ and $[\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}]_{\mathrm I}=1.76\times10^{-3}/(9.62\times10^{-3})=0.183$M.

problems.title: 6. Stereochemistry of two isomeric hydrocarbons
problems.statement: Two isomeric hydrocarbons A and B contain85.7mass% carbon.

sections.title: Tasks

parts.statement:
Write a general formula satisfying this condition.

A and B have these properties. Ozone treatment followed by zinc dust in acid gives a single organic product C from either. Oxidation of C gives a single carboxylic acid D. Spectral data place all hydrogen atoms of D, except the carboxyl hydrogen, in methyl groups. Vapour density of D corrected to normal conditions($0\,{}^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$,1atm) is $9.1\ \mathrm{g\,dm^{-3}}$.

A is more reactive than B with cold neutral potassium permanganate. A gives single compound F; B gives a1:1mixture of isomers G1,G2.
Draw structural formulae of D in aqueous solution and vapour phase.
Write the formula of C.
Draw structures of A and B.
a) Write reactions transforming A or B into C and D. b) Write reactions transforming A,B into F,G1,G2.
G1,G2 readily react with acetone in acid, forming H1,H2. Draw H1,H2.

A and B react with bromine. One product is non-polar(practically zero dipole moment) and optically inactive. Draw its stereochemical formula and formation reaction. Determine any chiral atoms' absolute configuration and mark them R or S.

Alkenes react with peroxoacids, adding oxygen to the double bond to form a three-member oxygen-containing ring. Epoxidation is highly stereospecific, retaining relative substituent positions at the bond. A with peroxoacetic acid gives single compound K. B under the same conditions gives1:1isomers L1,L2.
Is K optically active? Draw K's stereochemical formula. Are individual L1,L2 optically active? Draw their stereochemical formulae.

problems.title: 7. Norbornene-dicarboxylic acid stereochemistry
problems.statement:
Stereochemistry can sometimes be determined by studying chemical behaviour. One isomer of5-norbornene-2,3-dicarboxylic acids(compound X) has the following structure, with no stereochemistry shown:

![](p7-fig1)

Heating decomposes X to water and new compound Y. Y slowly dissolves in excess aqueous NaOH to give X1, identical to the product of X with NaOH. Treating the X1 solution with iodine gives iodine-containing compounds. Acidification yields isomeric A,B in3:1ratio. Titration of0.3913g A with0.1000M NaOH using phenolphthalein requires $12.70\ \mathrm{cm^3}$ alkali. The same volume is needed for0.3913g B. Heating slowly transforms A to C, which contains no iodine and can react with water. B does not transform under the same conditions, but heating with hydrochloric acid slowly converts B to A.

**All reactions must be written as balance equations. No mechanisms are required.**
